case_study_insert.main_stem: Thorncombe Belting (THB) is a cooperative in the conveyor belting sector, manufacturing steel-cord conveyor belts and power transmission belts for mining and agriculture, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2002 by Thandi Mokoena, the cooperative operates a flat structure with democratic leadership and is based in Rustenburg, South Africa. THB plans to invest $920,000 in a new calendering line for steel-cord belts, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and a $320,000 share issue to members. It has fixed costs of $405,000 a year, a variable cost of $27.00 a unit and a selling price of $45.00, and currently produces 36,000 units a year. THB faces a serious skills problem: a wave of retirements has left a shortage of qualified rubber calendering technicians across the shop floor.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The calendering line produced 9,250 belts last quarter at a waste rate of 5.6%, up from 3.9% a year ago. Customer complaints rose from 7 to 15 per month. On-time delivery stands at 91.8%. A rooftop solar array trial cut grid electricity use by 22% during daylight shifts. A market research survey of 180 mining and farm managers found that 77% prefer locally reinforced steel-cord belts and 53% would accept a 5% price premium for a 10-year wear warranty. A skills-gap audit shows 17 of 52 staff lack certified rubber-calendering qualifications; off-the-job certification courses at the industry academy cost $1,100 per employee.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 6.00% to 6.75%, the sixth rise this year, increasing repayment costs on variable-rate cooperative loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.5% from $11.00 to $11.72 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills in heavy industry. (3) Natural rubber and steel cord input costs have risen 14.6% year-on-year, industrial inflation is running at 9.1%, and mining production grew 4.2% in the same period.

questions.question_text: THB plans to finance part of its calendering-line expansion with a share issue to members. Explain two advantages for THB of using a member share issue instead of relying entirely on the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A member share issue keeps capital inside the cooperative and reduces THB's dependence on the $600,000 bank loan, lowering fixed interest commitments while fixed costs already total $405,000 a year. Member capital also strengthens the cooperative's balance sheet at a time when input costs for natural rubber and steel cord are rising 14.6%, giving THB more room to negotiate without breaching loan covenants.

Point 2: Shares issued to members bind the workforce to the cooperative's long-term success — members who hold equity are more likely to stay, train and invest effort, which directly supports closing the calendering skills gap. It also spreads the $920,000 expansion risk across the membership rather than concentrating it with one lender, preserving democratic control: no bank acquires decision rights over THB's strategy, so Thandi Mokoena and the members remain in charge of how the new line is staffed and prioritised.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Thorncombe Belting and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: THB is launching its locally reinforced steel-cord belt range. Consider sponsoring the national mining summit, advertising in a mining trade magazine, or producing case-study videos for social media. Which should THB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Mining summit sponsorship: Sponsoring the national mining summit puts THB directly in front of mine engineers, procurement officers and farm-machinery managers in one venue, ideal for showcasing 10-year wear-warranty belts and the local reinforcing angle that 77% of the 180 surveyed managers prefer. The drawbacks are sponsorship fees, staffing and logistics for an event several hundred kilometres from Rustenburg, no guarantee that the right decision-makers stop at the stand, and a single day of visibility that cannot sustain awareness between events.

Mining trade magazine advertising: A full-page advert with technical wear data reaches professional readers across South Africa and neighbouring mines, building credibility over a long 12-month shelf life. However, print lead times are slow, effectiveness is hard to measure, and the premium for full-page colour is steep for a cooperative whose fixed costs already run at $405,000 a year; coverage also includes readers who will never specify conveyor belts.

Case-study videos for social media: Short films showing the calendering line, a mine's uptime gains and the solar array trial (22% daylight electricity saving) can run on LinkedIn and YouTube, targeting the 53% willing to pay a 5% premium and the 77% preferring locally reinforced belts. Production is inexpensive for industrial storytelling, measurable through views and enquiries, and reusable across sales proposals — though reach depends on disciplined posting and paid boosting to mine-specific audiences.

Recommendation: THB should choose case-study videos for social media. It showcases the local reinforcement and solar story authentically, costs far less than the summit, scales beyond any single venue, and measurably targets the premium-accepting managers in its research. The summit sponsorship is rejected as too expensive and one-off for a $920,000 expansion; the trade magazine advertisement is rejected as slow and unmeasurable for an industrial audience now living on digital channels; THB should cut three videos — uptime, warranty and member craftsmanship — and follow every enquiry with a site visit offer.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of THB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of THB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the summit sponsorship and trade magazine are rejected.

questions.question_text: THB's retirement wave has left 17 of 52 staff without certified rubber-calendering qualifications. Explain two benefits for THB of introducing profit sharing for its members.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Profit sharing gives members a direct financial stake in reducing the 5.6% waste rate and the 15 complaints a month that are eroding THB's cooperative surplus. When calendering technicians see that efficiency gains flow into a shared distribution, they are more likely to flag machine drift, tighten seam tolerances and mentor apprentices — protecting output of 36,000 units and supporting the business case for the $920,000 calendering line.

Point 2: Profit sharing reinforces the cooperative ethos that underpins THB's flat, democratic structure: members receive rewards as co-owners, not merely as employees. This strengthens commitment and retention at exactly the moment skilled calenders are retiring, makes THB more attractive to young recruits choosing between factory jobs, and reduces the need for external supervision — preserving the low-hierarchy culture while raising accountability for quality, attendance and continuous improvement across 52 members.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to THB's skills gap, waste, quality and cooperative model.

questions.question_text: THB's coordination is straining as the calendering line prepares to start. Consider keeping its flat democratic structure or appointing a full-time operations manager with authority over shifts. Which should THB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Keeping the flat democratic structure: Retaining member-elected, democratic shift leadership preserves the cooperative's identity, keeps decision-making close to the work, and holds member engagement high while 17 of 52 staff retrain. Motivation and ownership remain strong, and there is no added hierarchy salary. The risks are real, however: slower coordination across three shifts, unclear accountability when quality drifts, informal power among longer-serving members, and leadership bandwidth that Thandi Mokoena may already be stretching thin during a $920,000 expansion.

Appointing a full-time operations manager: A dedicated manager would own shift planning, waste targets, safety on the new calender and delivery performance against mining customers, lifting the 91.8% on-time delivery record. It provides a single accountable point for the 15 monthly complaints and for coordinating with the industry academy on certification. The risks are equally clear: an added layer contradicts the cooperative's flat, democratic constitution unless members vote it in, may demotivate experienced members who resist top-down direction, and costs a senior salary that tightens the $405,000 fixed-cost line just as rubber inflation bites.

Decision: THB should keep its flat democratic structure for now and appoint a member coordinator pair — two elected technicians with defined shift-authority — rather than an outside hierarchical manager. This strengthens coordination without breaking the cooperative constitution, costs far less than an external appointment, and directly accelerates skills transfer while 17 members retrain. A full-time operations manager is rejected at this stage because it risks member disengagement and added fixed cost before the new calender proves its output; THB should review the decision in 12 months, and if on-time delivery and waste targets are still failing after full certification, a member vote can then consider a dedicated manager with clearly bounded authority.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two organisational approaches with limited application to THB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the advantages and disadvantages of one or both approaches in the context of THB.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches in the context of THB with a well-justified decision covering coordination, motivation, cost and cooperative governance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how THB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $405,000 ÷ ($45.00 − $27.00) = $405,000 ÷ $18.00 = 22,500 units. Answer: break-even output is 22,500 units a year.

Formula: Labour productivity = Total output ÷ Number of employees. Substitution: 36,000 units ÷ 52 employees = 692.3 units per employee a year (≈692 units). Answer: labour productivity is about 692 units per employee a year.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways THB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 22,500-unit break-even output with actual output of 36,000 units to confirm the belt line is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 13,500 units, informing whether the new calender can absorb mining-sector demand growth of 4.2% without new shifts.
2. Contribution per unit of $18.00 lets THB model the 5% premium the 53% of managers will pay for a 10-year wear warranty, lifting the price to $47.25, letting managers judge whether warranty reserves still protect the $405,000 fixed costs and the $600,000 bank loan instalments.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $405,000 and contribution per unit helps managers set the volume threshold needed before the $320,000 member share issue money is fully deployed, checking the expanded line can service both the loan and member dividends before approving overtime.
4. Labour productivity of about 692 units per employee a year gives THB a baseline to measure the new calender's impact: if the retrained 17 technicians lift units per member, unit cost falls ($405,000 ÷ 36,000 units + $27.00 = $38.25 a unit), rewarding profit sharing and funding the 10-year warranty exposure on the belts sold.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 22,500 units | (ii) labour productivity ≈ 692 units per employee a year | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 13,500 units against 36,000-unit output; pricing the 5% premium at $47.25; loan and share-issue feasibility on $405,000 fixed costs; and unit-cost benchmarking at $38.25 to measure the retrained calender crew's productivity.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate THB's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has THB's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.60 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.65 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.09 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 inventories + $260,000 trade receivables + $90,000 cash = $560,000; 2025 current assets = $225,000 + $300,000 + $135,000 = $660,000. 2024 = $560,000 ÷ $350,000 = 1.60; 2025 = $660,000 ÷ $400,000 = 1.65. Quick cover 2024 = ($560,000 − $210,000) ÷ $350,000 = $350,000 ÷ $350,000 = 1.00; 2025 = ($660,000 − $225,000) ÷ $400,000 = $435,000 ÷ $400,000 = 1.09.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened and now stands well clear of danger. Short-term cover improved from 1.60 to 1.65 while quick cover climbed from 1.00 to 1.09 — the 2024 position was exactly at the edge of relying on stock sales to meet short-term bills, whereas 2025 meets every $1 of short-term debt with roughly $1.09 of liquid assets. Cash rose strongly from $90,000 to $135,000, a reassuring buffer while THB implements the $920,000 calendering line and absorbs 14.6% rubber inflation. The cautions are receivables rising from $260,000 to $300,000 on longer mining-contract payment terms, inventories edging up $15,000 ahead of commissioning, and current liabilities up $50,000 — together signalling that growth is being part-financed by trade creditors, which can unwind fast if a mining customer disputes belt quality.

Conclusion: THB's financial position has improved. Short-term cover (1.60 to 1.65) and quick cover (1.00 to 1.09) show stronger solvency, and the buffer no longer depends on selling steel-cord belts from stock. The residual risks are the $40,000 receivables rise and the heavier liability base, so THB should negotiate progressed payments on mine contracts, keep the warranty reserve funded, and maintain the 22% daylight solar saving to protect cash during the line's ramp-up year.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables, cash and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether THB's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for THB of powering the new calendering line with solar renewable energy.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: THB's rooftop solar trial already shows a 22% cut in grid electricity use during daylight shifts, proving the technology works on its plant. Extending solar to the new calendering line would reduce operating costs for an energy-hungry process, strengthen THB's appeal to mining customers with their own decarbonisation targets, and build a genuine sustainability story for the 53% of managers willing to pay a 5% premium for warranties — while signalling cooperative leadership to members who value the local solar transition.

Disadvantage: Solar installation requires significant upfront capital on top of the $920,000 line itself, diverting member share issue funds approved for production equipment. Output is also intermittent: calendering needs steady pressure and temperature, so any shortfall must be covered by grid purchases, limiting actual savings. Maintenance of panels in a dusty industrial site adds cost, and if the trial's 22% saving does not scale to full calendar loads, THB could find its premium warranty pricing undermined by higher-than-expected energy costs and a longer recovery across the whole expansion.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to THB's solar trial, research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.75%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the 14.6% rise in input costs will affect THB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (6.00% to 6.75%): If THB's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.75% × $600,000 = $4,500 a year (0.0075 × $600,000) to interest costs — meaningful but modest against fixed costs of $405,000 a year, and zero if the cooperative fixed its rate at signing. The bigger exposure is psychological: higher rates chill mining-customer capital spending and make any second calender or a future member loan costlier, so THB should confirm its loan rate before board sign-off and avoid drawing the overdraft version of this risk wherever possible.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $11.72 per hour from April 2026): With 52 members mostly on hourly shop-floor rates, the rise is unavoidable. The insert gives no hours or pay split, so no defensible annual total can be invented; the honest benchmark is productivity: 36,000 units ÷ 52 staff ≈ 692 units per member a year. If the retrained calendering crew lifts that figure, the cooperative absorbs the rise through output; if not, unit labour cost climbs and the $18.00 contribution per unit shrinks, directly pressuring the $600,000 loan service that the expansion depends on.

Input cost inflation (14.6% natural rubber and steel cord): THB's $27.00 variable cost is dominated by these inputs, but the insert never decomposes it, so only an illustrative bound is defensible: if the whole variable cost rose 14.6% it would add 14.6% × $27.00 = $3.94 per unit (0.146 × $27.00 = $3.942); at 36,000 units a year that is about $141,912 (0.146 × $27.00 × 36,000). Even a milder illustrative $2.00 per unit would strip roughly $72,000 a year. Mining demand grew 4.2%, which helps volume, but rubber inflation compounds on every belt produced and is not removable by members' effort or solar panels.

Conclusion: The 14.6% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It multiplies across all 36,000 units, compresses the $18.00 contribution per unit, cannot be negotiated away by one year's belt contract, and directly pressures the $600,000 bank loan service and the 10-year wear-warranty pricing that justifies the line. The minimum wage rise is second, absorbable through productivity gains from the 17 retrained technicians; the interest rate rise is smallest at about $4,500 a year on a variable $600,000 loan. THB should lock rubber supply contracts for 2027, enforce the 5% premium on warranty belts, and use mining growth of 4.2% to dilute unit overheads before raising member distributions.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to THB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on THB's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of THB with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
